Pollute
puh-LOOT
v.
Latin polluere, to defile or soil, from por- (forth) + luere (to smear). In the KJV the smearing is moral and ceremonial: what God has made holy is dragged into common or filthy use.

Biblical Definition

To pollute in Scripture is to defile what God has declared holy—to take a thing set apart and treat it as common or filthy. The objects of the verb are almost always God's own: His sabbaths, His sanctuary, His altar, His name, His land, His covenant. My sabbaths they greatly polluted (Ezek 20:13) is the charge against a rebel generation. The priests of Malachi's day polluted the altar with contemptible offerings and then asked innocently, Wherein have we polluted thee? (Mal 1:7). Zephaniah's indictment is blunt: her priests have polluted the sanctuary, they have done violence to the law (Zeph 3:4). The land itself can be polluted, and by a specific sin: ye shall not pollute the land wherein ye are: for blood it defileth the land: and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood that is shed therein, but by the blood of him that shed it (Num 35:33)—innocent blood stains ground, and only justice removes the stain. Notice what pollution is not in the Bible: it is not primarily dirt, disease, or environmental damage. It is a relational and covenantal category. A thing is polluted when it is used against the purpose for which God sanctified it, and the pollution attaches to worship, to marriage, to the priesthood, to the name of God, and to the ground itself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines POLLUTE as to make foul or unclean; to defile; and specifically to profane—to apply to a common purpose that which is holy, or to violate by irreverence.

expand to see more

POLLUTE, v.t. — To make foul or unclean; to defile; in a general sense.

POLLUTE, v.t. — To taint with guilt; to profane; to use for a common purpose what is holy or set apart. They polluted my sabbaths (Ezek 20:13). Also, to violate by illegal sexual commerce.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 20:13 — "But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness: they walked not in my statutes, and they despised my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; and my sabbaths they greatly polluted: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them in the wilderness, to consume them."

Malachi 1:7 — "Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the LORD is contemptible."

Zephaniah 3:4 — "Her prophets are light and treacherous persons: her priests have polluted the sanctuary, they have done violence to the law."

Modern Corruption

Pollution has been narrowed to an environmental measurement, so that a culture can speak fluently about polluted air and have no words at all for a polluted altar, a polluted marriage bed, or a land defiled by innocent blood.

expand to see more

The modern word is a matter of parts per million. Pollution is what industry does to water; it is measured, regulated, and morally weightless apart from the statute. Scripture's pollution is a covenant category—something holy dragged into common use—and it cannot be measured by instruments at all. The narrowing is convenient: a society that only recognizes chemical defilement can pride itself on clean rivers while its worship, its marriages, and its courts are precisely what the prophets called polluted.

A second corruption is the confident denial that anything can be defiled, because nothing is holy in the first place. If the sabbath is a preference, it cannot be profaned; if marriage is a contract, it cannot be defiled; if the sanctuary is a building, it cannot be polluted. Malachi's priests were more sophisticated than that. They did not deny the categories; they asked, Wherein have we polluted thee?—the tone of men who kept the vocabulary and had stopped believing the substance, which is nearer to the church's present danger than open denial.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chalal, to profane or make common, and tame, to make unclean—the two verbs behind sabbaths profaned, sanctuaries defiled, and land stained by blood.

expand to see more

Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, defile, make common; used of profaning the sabbath, the sanctuary, the priesthood, and the name of God (Lev 19:8; Ezek 20:13; 22:26).

Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or become unclean, to defile ceremonially or morally (Lev 11:44; Num 35:34; Ezek 20:31).

Hebrew chaneph (H2610) — to be profaned or polluted, especially of land defiled by bloodshed (Num 35:33; Ps 106:38; Isa 24:5).

Usage

"My sabbaths they greatly polluted—pollution in Scripture attaches first to holy things."

"Wherein have we polluted thee? is the voice of men who kept the words and lost the substance."

"Numbers 35:33: innocent blood defiles the ground, and only justice cleanses it."
